body.heading: Plan the replacement, not the ban
paragraphs: A screen-free evening announced as a rule often becomes an argument about the rule. It works better as an offer: tonight we are doing something specific instead. A card tournament, a baking project, a walk with torches. The activity is the headline, not the absence of phones.
Keep it short and bounded. One evening a week, or just the hour after dinner, is easier to agree to than a whole weekend. When the end time is clear, people relax into it instead of counting down.

body.heading: Make the start easy
paragraphs: Put the materials out before the evening begins: cards on the table, ingredients on the counter, board game already open. The first five minutes decide most evenings, and a visible starting point beats a discussion about what to do.
Phones rest in one agreed place, like a basket by the door, and adults follow the same rule as children. Nothing kills the mood faster than one person scrolling while everyone else plays.

body.heading: Let it be ordinary
paragraphs: Not every screen-free evening needs to be memorable. Some will be a bit flat, and that is fine. The point is a regular pocket of time where the household is in the same room, doing the same thing, at nobody's pace but its own.
Start this week, with whatever is already in the house. The first ordinary evening is the one that makes the second one easier to suggest.

description: An evening without screens goes better when something replaces them, not when they are simply banned.
